prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

O blithe New-comer! I have heard, I hear thee and rejoice. O Cuckoo! shall I call thee Bird, Or but a wandering Voice? While I am lying on the grass Thy twofold shout I hear; From hill to hill it seems to pass, At once far off, and near. Though babbling only to the Vale Of sunshine and of flowers, Thou bringest unto me a tale Of visionary hours. Thrice welcome, darling of the Spring! Even yet thou art to me No bird, but an invisible thing, A voice, a mystery; The same whom in my school-boy days I listened to; that Cry Which made me look a thousand ways In bush, and tree, and sky. To seek thee did I often rove Through woods and on the green; And thou wert still a hope, a love; Still longed for, never seen. And I can listen to thee yet; Can lie upon the plain And listen, till I do beget That golden time again. O blessèd Bird! the earth we pace Again appears to be An unsubstantial, faery place; That is fit home for Thee!

outputs.L2:
Joyful new arrival, I have caught your sound—yes, I hear you, and it fills me with gladness. Cuckoo, should I name you a bird, or only a roaming voice?

As I rest upon the grass, your double call reaches me. It appears to travel from one hill to another, sounding both distant and close at the same moment.

Though you seem to chatter only to the sunny, flower-filled valley, you bring me a message from hours shaped by imagination and vision.

You are welcome three times over, beloved sign of spring. Even now, to me, you are not truly a bird, but something unseen—a sound, a wonder, a mystery.

You are the very same presence I listened for when I was a schoolboy: that cry which made me search everywhere—in bushes, among trees, and across the sky.

Many times I wandered through groves and over the grass trying to find you. Yet you remained always a hope, an object of affection—always desired, but never actually seen.

Still, even now, I can listen to you. I can lie down upon the open ground and keep listening until I bring back that bright, golden season of the past.

Blessed bird, the world we walk upon seems once more to become unreal and enchanted—a fairy-like place, perfectly suited to be your dwelling.
outputs.L3:
The speaker listens with joy to the call of the cuckoo, greeting it as a welcome sound of spring. Yet the bird remains mysterious to him. He wonders whether it is truly a living bird nearby or simply a wandering voice moving through the air. Because he cannot see the cuckoo, its presence feels almost magical, as though it belongs partly to the natural world and partly to the world of imagination.

The cuckoo’s repeated, twofold cry seems to travel across the landscape. At one moment, it sounds far away; at another, it appears close at hand. This shifting quality makes the call difficult to locate and deepens the speaker’s sense of wonder. The sound fills the valleys, hills, and fields, creating the impression that the cuckoo is everywhere and nowhere at once.

The call also awakens memories of the speaker’s childhood. As a boy, he used to hear the same mysterious cry and search eagerly for the hidden bird that made it. He wandered through the countryside, hoping to discover its source, but the cuckoo always remained unseen. This childhood experience made the bird seem even more enchanting, like a secret presence hidden within nature.

Although the cuckoo never appears before him, it continues to stir powerful feelings in the speaker. Its voice brings him hope, affection, and delight. The unseen bird becomes more than an ordinary creature; it becomes a symbol of mystery, memory, and the lasting power of nature to move the human heart.

By listening to the cuckoo, the speaker feels that the world has become magical and dreamlike once again. The familiar landscape is transformed into a place of beauty and mystery, just as it seemed in childhood. The cuckoo’s call restores his sense of wonder, allowing him to experience nature with renewed joy and imagination.
outputs.L4:
Wordsworth’s poem presents the cuckoo not simply as a bird, but as a mysterious and almost supernatural presence associated with spring, memory, and imagination. The speaker hears the cuckoo’s call in the present moment, yet the sound immediately carries him beyond ordinary experience. Because the bird remains unseen, it seems less like a physical creature than a wandering voice moving through the air. This disembodied call gives the cuckoo an enchanted quality, making it appear to belong both to the natural world and to the realm of dream, vision, and childhood wonder.

As the speaker listens, the cuckoo’s voice awakens memories of his early life. In childhood, he had searched for the bird and imagined it in many places, but he could never fully find or possess it. This memory is important because it shows how the cuckoo became, for him, a symbol of longing and imaginative desire. The bird’s call suggested something beautiful and distant, something always present yet always just beyond reach. In this way, the cuckoo represents the kind of mystery that excited the child’s imagination and made the natural world feel alive with hidden meaning.

The poem also contrasts adult perception with childhood vision. As an adult, the speaker hears the cuckoo again and is transported back to the freshness of his earlier experience. The sound restores, at least for a moment, a “golden” view of the world, in which nature seems magical, radiant, and full of possibility. Ordinary earth is transformed by the bird’s call into a place of wonder. Fields, hills, and valleys are no longer merely familiar landscapes; they become part of an enchanted world shaped by memory and imagination.

Through this experience, Wordsworth suggests that nature has the power to revive deep feelings that time might seem to have buried. The cuckoo’s song reconnects the speaker with his childhood self and with a more visionary way of seeing. Although the bird remains unseen, its voice is powerful enough to awaken joy, longing, and spiritual wonder. The poem therefore celebrates the enduring influence of nature on the human mind, showing how a simple sound in spring can open a path back to innocence, imagination, and a heightened sense of life.
outputs.L5:
The cuckoo is a fascinating bird known for its unique behavior and distinctive call. In many places, the sound of a cuckoo is seen as a sign of a new season, especially spring. This bird is often recognized by its soft gray feathers, long tail, and clear, repeated “cuckoo” sound.

One of the most interesting facts about the cuckoo is the way it raises its young. Instead of building its own nest, some cuckoo species lay their eggs in the nests of other birds. The other bird then cares for the cuckoo chick as if it were its own. This unusual behavior makes the cuckoo one of the most remarkable birds in nature.

Whether heard in the forest or seen flying across open land, the cuckoo always brings a sense of curiosity and wonder. For many people, spotting a cuckoo or hearing its call feels like discovering something new in the natural world.
